22206-an-old-meerschaum-from-coals-of-fi:
An Old Meerschaum is one of the tales in David Christie Murray's Coals of Fire and Other Stories. The story opens on a pretty young lady in the street. Two minutes later comes a young gentleman who seems her refined copy, save in one point. Where she is demure, impudence and mischief shine from him like light from a lantern.

That brother-and-sister contrast sets the tale moving. A meerschaum pipe, smoked and coloured by years, links the characters to an older generation's story. Murray was a practised hand at the magazine short story. His Coals of Fire tales mix sentiment, coincidence, and shrewd character in the approved Victorian mixture.
22256-sparkling-gems-of-race-knowledge-w:
Sparkling Gems of Race Knowledge Worth Reading compresses a library of Black achievement into one small compendium. Its editors launch the book with a plain hope: to instruct and encourage the coloured people. They claim to have packed a vast amount of valuable race information into a small compass. The style is good and the moral tone excellent, they promise, and every family should own it.

Inside stand sketches of Black leaders, poets, soldiers, businessmen, and inventors. Facts, speeches, and poems answer the slanders of the Jim Crow age with evidence. Such race books were sold door to door across the South. This one shows the self-help literature Black readers built for themselves.
22478-the-priest-s-tale-pe-re-etienne-fr:
Robert Keable wrote The Priest's Tale, Pere Etienne, for the New Decameron. Its narrator disclaims clairvoyance at the start of his story. He dislikes that jargon, he says firmly and plainly.

Yet he knew, he insists, whenever Pere Etienne passed his door. Even through the smoke-room door, the priest's presence registered on him. He sensed it while about to play a doubled four in no trumps. That bridge-table detail grounds the uncanny feeling in club life. Keable mixes war, faith, and quiet mystery in the tale. Readers meet a priest whose presence seems to reach through walls. The story leaves its wonder unexplained and understated.
belgium:
Joseph E. Morris's Belgium, a volume in the Beautiful Europe series, opens by apologizing for its own title. It needs an effort of imagination, he writes, to think of Belgium as beautiful Europe at this hour. The cockpit of the Continent is accomplishing its frightful destiny. No treaty, no scrap of paper, can save the weakest nation of Western Europe from drinking the cup of ruin. Morris wrote as the German invasion of 1914 made his travel book an elegy.

Inside, the tour proceeds city by city through the Belgium of the guidebooks: churches, belfries, lace, and canals, now read against the news. His chapters on Bruges, Ghent, and Brussels carry a double exposure of art and war. Readers get a minor classic of unintended history: a belle-époque travel portrait overtaken, between writing and printing, by the event that made Belgium a byword.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-limina-apo: Ad limina apostolorum names the pilgrimage to Rome's sepulchres of St. Peter and St. Paul. The journey runs to the Prince of the Apostles' basilica and to St. Paul's basilica outside the walls. The entry gives this brief definition of the Roman pilgrimage and its two shrines, and nothing more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adytum:
Adytum, from adyton, a privative plus dyo, to enter, is a secret chamber, a place of retirement in ancient temples. Held most sacred, the innermost sanctuary or shrine, only officiating priests might enter, and oracles were given from this place.

Solomon's temple's Holy of Holies, or Sanctum Sanctorum, shared the pagan adytum's nature, since none but the high priest entered it, and he only once a year. Among Egyptians the secos was the same thing, as Strabo describes. A well-preserved adytum stands in the little temple at Pompeii, raised some steps above the temple floor and without light. In Christian architecture the word sometimes means a church's chancel, or altar end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agaunum:
Agaunum, today St. Maurice-en-Valais, in Sion's Swiss diocese, owes its fame to an event St. Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons, relates: the martyrdom of a Roman legion, the Theban Legion, early in the fourth century. For centuries this martyrdom passed as fact, but since the Reformation it has drawn long and violent controversies, recounted exactly in Franz Stolle's work.

Sources for the Theban martyrdom are few: two editions of their Acts, entries in calendars and martyrologies, and Eucherius's letter of 450. To these may be added Passiones of Theban martyrs who escaped Agaunum but later fell in Germany and Italy. Only under Theodore of Octodurum, bishop 369 to 391, long after the event, did attention turn to the massacre. Then, Eucherius says, a basilica rose for the martyrs, whose presence Theodore learned by revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amphilochius-:
Bishop of Iconium from early in 374, Amphilochius was a fourth-century churchman born in Cappadocia around 339 or 340. He was probably a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus. Trained for the law, he worked briefly as a barrister at Constantinople. He then left that career for religious life near Gregory, before Basil of Caesarea drew him into church affairs.

He is best remembered for defending the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonians. Basil dedicated his own treatise on the Spirit to him for that cause. Amphilochius wrote a similar work, now lost, and attended the Synod of Constantinople in 381. He left letters and fragments, some genuine and some wrongly ascribed to him, that still help scholars trace early teaching on the Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Borglum, in Denmark, embraced the ancient districts of Vendsyssel and Thy, the whole extreme north of Jutland beyond the Limfjord. The see began at Vestervig, formed out of Viborg on the death of Bishop Val in 1059. Magnus, first Bishop of Vestervig, drowned in the Elbe about 1060, returning home after consecration by Adalbert I of Hamburg.

Albrik, Dean of Bremen, served as second bishop from 1066 to 1085. Vestervig had sheltered Saint Thoger, a missionary from Thuringia and chaplain to Saint Olaf. He retired there after Olaf's death in 1030, built a church of thatch and wattle, and preached to the district. Thoger died on 24 June 1067 and was canonized despite the opposition of King Svend Estridsen and Bishop Albrik, becoming patron of the diocese. Bishop Sylvester moved the see in 1134 to 1136 to the Premonstratensian abbey of Borglum, whose canons formed the chapter that elected the bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anemurium: Anemurium, now called Estenmure, was a titular see of Cilicia, a church title preserving the name of an ancient diocese. In antiquity it stood on a high bluff knob marking the southernmost point of Asia Minor, facing Cyprus across the sea. Its ruins, including theatres, tombs, and walls, are still visible to visitors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antimensium:
Antimensium, also Antiminsion, Greek for instead of the altar, is a consecrated corporal used only in the Greek Rite. In Russian and Slavonic it is antimins, substantially the Roman Rite's portable altar. It is a strip of fine linen or silk, about ten by thirteen inches. It is ornamented with the Passion instruments or Our Lord in the Sepulchre. It contains saints' relics sewn in and certified by the bishop.

It must lie on the altar in Greek churches, as an altar-stone does in Latin churches; no Mass may be said without it. It is unfolded at the Offertory quite like the Latin corporal. Outside Mass it rests folded in four on the altar. Since 1842 each Russian church must register its antimensia exactly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcanum:
Arcanum is an encyclical on Christian marriage, issued by Leo XIII on 10 February 1880. Since family life is the seed of society and marriage the basis of family life, the health of civil and religious society depends on marriage. That health rests on the inviolability, or unbreakability, of the marriage contract. Christ's mission, it argues, was to restore humanity in the supernatural order, benefiting first the individual and then society as a whole.

From that principle the letter treats Christian marriage as sanctifying the family, society's unit. The marriage contract, set up by God, had from the start two properties, unity and indissolubility. Human weakness corrupted it over time: polygamy, many spouses, destroyed unity, and divorce destroyed indissolubility. Christ restored the original idea and, to sanctify the institution more fully, raised the marriage contract to sacramental dignity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcosolium:
An arcosolium, from arcus, arch, and solium, a word Latin writers sometimes used for sarcophagus, was one form of tomb in the Roman catacombs. An inscription published by Marchi still stands in the Palazzo Borghese courtyard. It records that Aurelius Celsus and Aurelia Hilaritas had this arcosolium with its little wall made for themselves and their friends, in peace. The tombs were cut in the soft tufa walls of the catacombs.

Builders first hollowed a space like an ordinary loculus, or wall niche, topped by an arch. Then they opened an oblong cavity downward into the rock facing the arch, and laid a marble slab horizontally over the opening. The tomb thus became a kind of sarcophagus hewn from living rock, its closing slab forming a table-like top beneath the arch. The entry gives a builder's view of how early Christians buried their dead in stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atrium:
In early church building, an atrium was a large open court set before the church itself. Covered walks ringed it on four sides, and worshippers crossed it between porch and nave. A fountain at its center let them wash their hands before going in, a custom that lives on in the holy-water font. Penitents stood there to ask prayers from those entering, and the court also served as a burial ground.

Famous early examples include old St Peter's in Rome and Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. The form survived in places such as St Clement's in Rome and St Ambrose in Milan. The entry adds a second, secular sense from Roman houses, where the atrium was the main entrance hall. There it was lit through a roof opening called the compluvium, with rain caught in a floor basin called the impluvium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-axum:
Axum, is a titular metropolitan see of ancient Christian Ethiopia, with bishops listed from the mid-fourth century to 650. Modern Axum, capital of the Tigre province of Abyssinia, nestles in a valley beneath an Adoua peak. It stands 7,545 feet above sea level. A plain below it feeds streams that run toward the Nile. A recent traveler describes a sacred enclosure, nearly a mile round, holding the cathedral, monastery, and the bishop's house.

The city is ancient. Greeks and Romans knew it with Adule as a trade center for gold dust, ivory, leather, hides, and aromatics from Africa's interior. Its people mix Ethiopic and Arab blood, and Himyaritic inscriptions nearby show Arabia's influence, as do stone monuments bearing sun and star worship. Greek coins older than the fourth century and Ethiopic coins titled Negush Aksum have been found there, and sixth-century Gheez inscriptions aid the history of the Semitic alphabet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belgium:
Belgium takes up a long historical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It traces the small kingdom through revolution, foreign rule, and independence. Its narrative runs from the French armies of 1794 through Dutch rule and the break of 1830, with the Church present at nearly every turn. Bishops, clergy, schools, and political parties all shape the story it tells.

Much of the entry follows the long fight over schools and the place of faith in public life, from state-run universities to laws on private and public teaching. It also covers the Catholic party in power, the growth of religious orders, and Belgian mission work abroad, including the Congo and India. Readers get a dense political and church history rather than a short gazetteer note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblia-pauper:
Biblia Pauperum, the Bible of the Poor, was a picture book pairing scenes from Christ's life with Old Testament foreshadowings, described in this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A series of forty or fifty pages, each divided into nine sections, puts the Gospel scene at the centre, prophets above and below, and Old Testament scenes at the sides.

Corner texts explain the links, making the book a picture concordance of the two Testaments, gathering the Church's traditional reading of types and figures as taught in liturgy and preaching. Though called the poor man's Bible, it likely served preachers and the literate too. The entry presents a medieval teaching aid in pictures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bullarium:
A Bullarium gathers bulls and similar papal documents, whether general or tied to one order, house, or place. The name came from the canonist Laertius Cherubini, whose 1586 folio of 1,404 pages held 922 papal constitutions from Gregory VII to the reigning Sixtus V. Later collections followed his model, but three cautions govern them all.

First, each editor chose by his own judgment, so no collection held official standing. The exception is Benedict XIV's first volume of his own bulls, sent to Bologna in 1746 as a source of law. Second, no collection claimed completeness, or even all constitutions of general interest. Third, editors meant at first to exclude pronouncements already inside canon law's corpus, aiming instead to rescue enactments the corpus compilers had missed or popes had issued since. Mazzutellus's 1579 volume of 723 documents shows the form before Cherubini fixed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caeremoniale-:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum is the book of rites and ceremonies for bishops and lesser prelates at Mass, Vespers, and other functions in metropolitan, cathedral, and collegiate churches. It also settles precedence among clergy and official layfolk. After Sixtus V set up the Congregation of Sacred Rites in 1587, Clement VIII had the book corrected and issued it in 1600.

Errors crept in, so Innocent X had it revised in 1650, Benedict XIII issued a new edition in 1727, and Benedict XIV published an amended and enlarged one in 1741 and 1752. A standard edition of 1886 now rules all others. Its first book covers the bishop's duties, dress, and ministers, and its second the Divine Office and Mass through the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarius-of-:
Caesarius of Prum, born of the noble Milendonk family, was abbot of the rich Benedictine house of Prum near Trier, elected in 1212. Prum then ranked among the richest monasteries in Europe, but many of its monks were noblemen living in comfort, and their example wore down discipline. After five years Caesarius gave up the abbacy to live a stricter life as a humble monk at the Cistercian house of Heisterbach.

At Abbot Kuno's request he wrote in 1222 a commentary on the Register of the Estates of Prum. Drawn up in 893, it has become a key source for thirteenth-century law and civilization. Leibniz and later editors printed the register with his commentary, and recent research also credits him with the history of the abbots of Prum, long assigned to Caesarius of Heisterbach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capharnaum:
Capharnaum, also called Kapernaum, was a town of Palestine whose name means village of Nahum, or consolation. The Gospels make it Jesus's home after rejection at Nazareth. There he called Peter, Andrew, James, John, and Matthew as disciples. There he healed a paralytic, Peter's mother-in-law, the centurion's servant, and others. There too he spoke the discourse on the Eucharist.

Its people, urged on by the Pharisees, broke with him, and on leaving he pronounced a curse on the city. Under Constantine a converted Jew named Count Joseph built a church there. Pilgrims visited it into the sixth century. After that the town fades from Palestinian history, surviving now only as a Latin titular see whose exact origin the entry leaves unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cariati-pater:
Cariati is a diocese of Calabria in the province of Cosenza, suffragan to Santa Severina, in a healthy site near the sea. Menecrates, present at the Roman synod of 499, is the first bishop on record. Gregory the Great later commended its church to the Bishop of Reggio. A union with the diocese of Cerenza in the eleventh or twelfth century is possible but first appears in record in 1342.

Noteworthy bishops include Polychronius, founder of a monastery at Santa Severina in 1099, and the Cistercian Matteo, who first led the abbey of San Giovanni di Fiore as abbot. The soldier turned nuncio Alessandro Crivello and Fra Filippo Gesualdo, who died in the odor of sanctity, also appear. Pius VII joined Strongoli and Umbriatico to the see in 1818, leaving a diocese of 60,000 people with 28 parishes, 70 churches and chapels, and 61 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casium:
Casium was a titular see of Lower Egypt near Pelusium, by the sandhills Greek geographers called Kasion Oros, today El-Katieh or El-Kas. A temple of Zeus Kasios, the Aramean god Qasiou, stood there, and Pompey, murdered nearby, was buried at the place. Geographers and church lists name it as a bishopric under Pelusium in Augustamnica Prima, from Georgius Cyprius and Hierocles to a notice of about 840.

Only one bishop is known, Lampetius, who attended Ephesus in 431. Cyril sent him with Hermogenes of Rhinocorura to Rome, where both attended the consecration of Pope Sixtus III. Many letters of Isidore of Pelusium are addressed to Lampetius, whose name survives through that correspondence and the council record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedraticum:
Cathedraticum is a yearly sum paid for the bishop's support, given as a mark of honor and a sign of submission to the cathedral church. In the early Church such gifts came by custom rather than law. The earliest law on the subject seems to be a Braga canon of 572. It bound only parish churches and chapters to pay, since the sacraments were then given in parish churches alone.

As other endowed churches and chapels multiplied, Pope Honorius III extended the duty to them as well. The sum was paid at the bishop's annual visitation. The ancient amount was fixed at two solidi, a solidus being one seventy-second of a pound of gold. Later rulings, including decisions of Propaganda, kept the payment a binding law for those concerned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrismarium: A short glossary entry on the chrismarium, a word with two church meanings. In the first sense it is the place in a church set apart for giving Confirmation, where the bishop anoints candidates. In the second sense it is a round jar, usually of silver or pewter, used to hold the holy oils for anointing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciborium:
An entry on the ciborium, a chalice-like vessel holding the Blessed Sacrament. Some derive the word from Latin cibus, food, for the heavenly bread it holds, while others trace it to Greek kiborion, cup, for its first shape. In early Christian times the term also meant the canopy crowning the altar, but modern liturgical use restricts it to the sacred vessel for reserving the consecrated species.

Today two vessels reserve the Sacrament: the pyx, a small round box for carrying it to the sick, and the ciborium, used for distributing Communion and keeping particles in the tabernacle. Shaped like a chalice with a round bowl, conical cover, and cross, it must be gold or silver, lined with gold within. It is blessed rather than consecrated, and veiled in white silk or cloth of gold while holding the Species. Only sacred ministers may handle it when full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-circesium:
Circesium, a titular see of Osrhoene, was founded under Diocletian and restored by Justinian. Today's identification is Abu Serai, a village on the Euphrates' left bank at the meeting of the Khabur. An older city called Sirhi had stood there before it. Benjamin of Tudela wrongly identified Circesium with Kharkamis, a Hittite capital.

The city was a bishopric in Osrhoene, suffragan to Edessa, and appears only in a list of about 840. Lequien names five bishops, from Jonas at Nicaea, mutilated in an earlier persecution, to Thomas in 553. Fourteen Jacobite bishops are also recorded, from 793 to 1042.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Loccum, in Hanover, a Cistercian abbey of the Minden diocese, was founded in 1163 by Count Wilbrand von Hallermund. From Volkenrode in Thuringia came its first monks, under Abbot Eccardus, placing it in the Morimond line from Citeaux. An old writer calls its site a place of horror and vast solitude haunted by robbers. After want and harsh neighbours, the monks tilled the land and taught the people the fear of God.

The abbey filled its place in Brunswick church life until Lutheranism swept Catholicism from the country. Its chief interest now lies in its buildings, almost perfectly preserved as a Protestant seminary. The cruciform church, built between 1240 and 1277, measures about 218 feet by 110, beside a fine cloister, refectory, chapter-house, sacristy, dormitory, and lay-brothers wing. The head of the house still bears the title of abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citharizum:
Citharizum, a titular see of Armenia, lay in Asthianene or Balabitene, north of Commagene and Mesopotamia, between Masius and Anti-Taurus. Justinian built a castle there with a garrison under a duke and placed the city in Armenia Quarta, the province he had just formed. In 613 it fell to Ashot, general of the Persian king Chosroes the Second.

Only one bishop is known: Marianus of Kitharizon, named in the records of the Trullan Council of 692. The city appears about 840 in Parthey's first Notitia as part of Armenia Quarta under Melitene's metropolis, it is identified with the modern village of Keterig.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collectarium:
Augustin Joseph Schulte's entry defines the collectarium, also called collectarius or orationale. It is the book that holds the Collects. In the Roman Missal, the word Statio often stands before the Introit of a Mass. It marks the church where clergy and people once gathered to celebrate the mysteries on a saint's day or feast.

Before walking in procession to that church, they met nearby to receive the pontiff. He recited a prayer called the Collect. The name may come from the assembled people, or from the prayer summing up all favors asked, or from its brief form of the feast's spirit. In time the name spread to prayers before the Epistle, to Secrets and Post-Communions, and to prayers of the Divine Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coracesium:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers Coracesium, a titular see of Asia Minor. Ptolemy places it not in Cilicia Tracheia but in Roman Pamphylia. It had belonged to Isauria, and from A.D. 74 probably fell within Lycia-Pamphylia. Its port was the Cilician pirates' chief centre. There Antiochus VII killed Diodorus Tryphon, and Pompey destroyed the pirates, levelling their fortress.

Coracesium became suffragan of Side, metropolis of Pamphylia Prima. Lequien mentions only four bishops, the first at Constantinople's Council in 381, the last in 681. The see still appears in the Notitiæ episcopatuum as late as the twelfth or thirteenth century. Today Coracesium is a little town of about 2,000 inhabitants, 500 Greeks, chief centre of a caza in Konia. Its Turkish name is Alaya. Armenians have disappeared, though the town ranked important in the Rupens' time. Curious ruins, walls, and ancient tombs survive, with many romantic stories attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotiaeum:
Cotiaeum, an ancient city of Phrygia Salutaris, claims Aesop as a native son and a long career as a Christian centre. Heresy took root there from the second century, and Socrates records its Novatian bishop. At first a suffragan of Synnada, it rose to an autocephalous archbishopric, then a metropolis with as many as thirteen suffragans.

Ten bishops appear in Lequien's list, the last in the fourteenth century, beginning with Cyrus, sent by Theodosius II after townsfolk slew four bishops. Ruins, a Byzantine castle, and a church survive from antiquity, and Timur sacked the town in 1402. Modern Kutaya, famed for earthenware, counts about 22,000 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crisium:
A diocesan entry describes Crisium, a Graeco-Slavonic rite diocese in Croatia centred on the little town of Krizevac, north-east of Zagreb. About 1600 many Serbs emigrated from Serbia and Bosnia into Croatia, where they joined earlier settlers called Wallachians. Through Bishop Dimitrovich of Agram, their leader Simeon Vratania gained a monastery and became bishop of the Catholic Serbs in 1611.

His successors stayed loyal to Rome despite schismatic propaganda and conflicts with Agram. In 1671 Bishop Paul Zorcic became vicar-general of Agram for Slavonic-rite Catholics. Only in 1777 did Pius VI re-establish the Uniat diocese as Crisium. Its bishops have resided at Krizevac ever since, serving a flock counted alongside 225,000 schismatics in the territory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curium:
A short entry describes Curium, a Cypriot titular see suppressed by the papal legate Pelagius in 1222. Legend says Koureus, son of Kinyras, founded Kourion on the south-west coast and settled Argives there in 1595 BC. The city became capital of one of the island's kingdoms.

On the ruined site stands the modern village of Episkopi, near the sea, where Cesnola found the antiquities now in New York's Metropolitan Museum. In the Middle Ages Episkopi passed first to the Ibelin family, then to the Venetian Cornaro, owners of rich sugar plantations. Curium's recorded bishops number only two: Zeno at Ephesus in 431, and Michael in 1051. The tomb of Saint Hermogenes is kept in its church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diaconicum:
An entry on the diaconicum, a word with two linked senses in the Greek Church. As a book it lays out the deacon's functions, and as prayers it names the orations for peace he says before the people. First of all, though, it meant an annex to the basilica where altar supplies were kept and preparations made for the sacrifice.

Prothesis, the small room for receiving the people's offerings, stands distinct from it, and the two commonly flank the apse. A great church's diaconicum majus held several rooms: a reception hall for the bishop, a treasury for vessels and books, and the diaconicum proper. Syrian examples rise two stories on a rectangular plan, and the form recurs in Byzantine churches, African basilicas, and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didascalia-ap:
The Didascalia Apostolorum claims to be the teaching of the apostles at the Council of Jerusalem. In truth it is a church manual put together in the third century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry untangles its tangled afterlife, from its first printing in Syriac in 1854. In 1900 scholars found an old Latin version, more than half of which has perished.

The first eight books of the later Apostolic Constitutions simply rework the Didascalia. Scholars can thus rebuild much of the lost Greek original by setting the two texts side by side. The entry leans on the 1906 edition by Funk, and it shows how a manual for early Christian conduct survived in fragments across three tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-docimium:
Docimium was a titular see in Phrygia, a region of Asia Minor. Its coins call its people Macedonians, so it must have been founded by Antigonos Dokimos. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its shifting names, from Dokimeion to Dokimion, and notes its fame for marble quarries. The site is now the village of Istcha Kara Hissar, northeast of Afion Kara Hissar.

Many Christian inscriptions later than Constantine have been found there. Synnada in Phrygia Salutaris held authority over Docimium, whose known bishops number six or seven between 344 and 879, plus one more from an inscription. The entry is a compact study in coins, quarries, and bishop lists fixing a lost city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominus-vobis:
Dominus Vobiscum, Latin for the Lord be with you, is an ancient greeting taken into the liturgy as a prelude to formal prayer. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces it to Scripture, to Ruth and Chronicles, and to Christ's promise in Matthew that he is with his people. Church use dates likely from apostolic times, and the Council of Braga named it in 563. It also stands in the Gelasian Sacramentary of the sixth or seventh century.

The phrase bears a deep weight, since the Lord's presence pledges divine protection and earnest of every good gift. The entry follows its place in Mass and office, showing how a few words open the Church's solemn prayers. For readers of the liturgy, it unpacks a greeting heard at every altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dorylaeum:
Dorylaeum, a titular see in Phrygia Salutaris, Asia Minor, was already an ancient city under Phrygia's kings. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets it at Karadja Hissar, six miles southwest of modern Eski Shehir. Near the end of the fourth century before Christ it moved to Shehir Euyuk, where it stayed through the Byzantine age. Known bishops number seven, spanning the fourth through the ninth century.

The most famous, Eusebius, denounced in turn the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches. As late as the twelfth century it still appears among Synnada's suffragans, before fading from record. Seljuk Turks took and destroyed the town about 1070, yet crusaders won a battle there on 1 July 1097, a date the entry preserves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durham-dunelm:
Durham is an ancient English diocese holding a unique place among bishoprics. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that its border position against Scotland led its bishops to take on political and constitutional roles beside their spiritual office. Their rights were peculiar and wide, and even today the Anglican bishop of Durham ranks above all English prelates save Canterbury, York, and London.

Its line runs back to the Anglo-Saxon see of Lindisfarne, which Saint Aidan founded in 635. Aidan came from Iona at the call of King Oswald of Northumbria to preach to the newly conquered heathen kingdom. He built his monastery on Holy Island, and the entry follows the see from Lindisfarne to Durham through its prince-bishops and their coins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
The ecclesiastical forum is the Church's judicial and coercive power, expressed in the Latin word for a place holding a tribunal of justice. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry argues that this power is plain from the constitution given by the divine founder. As a perfect society, the Church holds within herself all powers needed to guide her members to their appointed end, with a matching right to be obeyed.

That right is called jurisdiction, the source of all church action not drawn from the power of holy orders. It grounds church law, binding both outwardly and inwardly, and from apostolic times rulers have put it into practice. The entry notes that civil encroachment has in our day shrunk the forum in practice, though unwarrantably, to spiritual causes alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-d:
Eusebius of Dorylaeum was the layman turned bishop who led the orthodox fight first against Nestorius and then against Eutyches in the fifth century. Trained as an advocate at Constantinople, he publicly challenged a sermon by the chaplain of Nestorius in 423. Later he broke into a sermon by Nestorius himself to protest that the eternal Word had taken a second birth, of a woman, in the flesh. 

As bishop he then turned on his former friend Eutyches, charging him with false teaching before Flavian's synod at Constantinople in 448. Eutyches was condemned, but the council of Ephesus in 449, run by Dioscurus, deposed and banished both Flavian and Eusebius amid cries against him. Eusebius fled to Rome, appealed to Pope Leo, and at Chalcedon in 451 stood as accuser of Dioscurus. He also helped frame the definition of faith that cleared his own name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flabellum:
The flabellum is a liturgical fan of leather, silk, parchment, or feathers. Deacons waved it at the altar to keep insects from the Sacred Species and the priest. The Apostolic Constitutions of the fourth century already order two deacons to hold such fans. Latin use faded about the fourteenth century; Greek use continues to the present day.

Greek deacons receive the sacred fan at ordination and wave it from Offertory to Communion. Rich examples survive, like the thirteenth-century Kremsmünster fan shaped as a Greek cross. Fans also served as marks of honour: two are borne beside the pope on the sedia gestatoria. In 1902 Leo XIII gave the old Vatican fans to Mrs. Joseph Drexel of Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gesta-romanor:
The Gesta Romanorum was a medieval Latin collection of anecdotes, each paired with a moral reflection. It was most likely assembled by a priest late in the thirteenth century or early in the fourteenth. Older guesses that named Berchorius or Helinandus as its author no longer stand. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces how the book grew, spread, and reached print.

Each tale opened under a heading naming a virtue or a vice. It then told its story and closed with a moral reading, giving preachers ready examples for sermons. Copies multiplied across Western Europe with local additions, and split into three manuscript families. The first printed editions appeared between 1472 and 1475, and an enlarged Vulgate held 181 stories. Poets from Chaucer and Boccaccio to Shakespeare and Schiller later mined the same tales. Many of them survive today inside famous works of European literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hadrumetum:
North Africa's Hadrumetum, a Phoenician colony older than Carthage, served Hannibal as a base against Scipio at the end of the Second Punic War. It grew rich under Rome, when Trajan raised it to a colonia. By the third century's end it was capital of the new province of Byzacena. Justinian restored it after the Vandals as Justinianopolis.

Arabs afflicted it again, the Aghlabids rebuilt it in the eleventh century as Susa, Normans held it briefly in the twelfth, and France took it in 1881. Modern Susa counts 25,000 people with a museum, garrison, harbour, and oil wells nearby. The entry closes with nine known bishops between 255 and 551, the last being Primasius, whose works survive in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-birn:
Cologne Carthusian Heinrich Birnbaum, born in 1403, entered the order at thirty-two and became a reformer of houses by sheer example. Esteemed for scriptural and theological learning, he was made prior of Mont Saint André at Tournai only three years after entering, in 1438, and held that post eleven years.

Successive priorships at Wesel, Rettel, Trier, Diest, and Liège followed, each house's few abuses yielding to his restoration of St. Bruno's austere discipline, until ill health sent him back to Cologne in 1463. His last decade went to ascetic writings, including a defence of the Immaculate Conception. The entry warns against confusing him with his jurist uncle of the same name, dead in 1439.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-busem:
Hermann Busembaum was a German Jesuit moral theologian, born at Notteln in Westphalia in 1600 and dead at Münster in 1668. He joined the Society of Jesus at nineteen, taught classics, philosophy, and moral and dogmatic theology, and served as rector of the colleges at Hildesheim and Münster. He also became confessor and trusted adviser to Christoph Bernard von Galen, the prince-bishop of Münster.

His lasting fame rests on one short book, the Medulla theologiae moralis, first issued in the mid-1600s. It packs a wide range of moral teaching into a small volume, set out in a clear and orderly way for priests facing hard cases of conscience. Later writers kept adding notes to it, which shows how widely priests used it. Readers meet here a teacher prized for sound judgment, plain method, and practical help.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homiliarium:
A homiliarium is a collection of homilies, familiar explanations of the Gospels, read with the recitation of the Divine Office. From very early times the Fathers' homilies stood in high esteem for this purpose. Gregory the Great refers to the custom, and Benedict mentions it in his rule, proving it as old as the sixth century.

Homilies of Leo I, terse and suited to liturgy, were prized above others. As new feasts entered the Office, demand for homilies grew, and by the eighth century, the age of liturgical codification, collections began to appear. Many homiliaria survive, and medieval references name many more, including a very old Gallican collection, one by the Roman priest Agimundus, and one compiled in England by Bede.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iconium:
Iconium was a titular see of Lycaonia, which Xenophon calls the easternmost town of Phrygia, while Cicero, Ammianus, and others place it in Lycaonia or Galatia, since provincial boundaries often changed. Anthony gave it to Polemon, dynast of Olbe, who reigned from 39 to 26 BC, and it later joined the Roman province of Galatia, becoming a colony under Claudius.

Paul preached there on his first mission and converted many Jews and pagans, returning soon after to organize the church he had founded, and he elsewhere recalls persecutions endured there. Thecla was one of his converts. Christianized early, Iconium hosted a council in 235 decreeing heretical baptism invalid. Le Quien names thirty-six bishops down to 1721, best known being Amphilochius, friend of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-partibus-i:
An entry on a Latin phrase that once followed the title of a bishop who held a see he could not live in. The phrase means “in the lands of the unbelievers,” and it was added to the names of old Christian sees that had fallen under non-Christian rule. Such bishops were called titular bishops, and the entry sets out how the practice grew.

Early bishops driven out by invaders kept their titles. Other churches gave them shelter. Some even ran empty sees for a time. Later the Church kept the names of lost sees alive by giving them to helper bishops and to bishops in mission lands. The entry traces that shift and dates regular titular appointments to the time of the Twelfth Lateran Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-invitatorium:
An invitation to the faithful to join the Divine Office opens this liturgy entry, which takes its name from that call to prayer. Psalm 95, the Venite, has served as the invitation from the earliest times. The life of Porphyrius of Gaza pictures him having it sung so the people could join in, answering Alleluia after each verse. Benedictine practice made it a daily fixture.

In the Benedictine night office the Venite opens the nocturns and is never left out. The antiphons sung with it shift with feasts and weekdays, repeated twice before the psalm and once after the Gloria Patri. Benedict's Rule calls the psalm the Invitatorium, while an older Frankish rule calls it the exhortation response. Readers get a small chant's long history in one place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-itinerarium:
A prayer for setting out on a journey, printed at the Breviary's end for easy finding, is the itinerarium treated here. Monks and clerics used it before travel, and the custom likely grew from monastic rule. Desert fathers Anthony and Pachomius, and Basil too, legislated in detail how monks should behave abroad, with set duties and restraints for the road.

Benedict's rule shaped Western church custom more than any other. In chapter 67 it ordered that brethren sent on a journey first commend themselves to the abbot's and community's prayers. The community remembered them daily while away. Short absences brought their own customs, the entry notes. Readers get a small prayer set inside a whole discipline of traveling as a monk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk von Nussbaum was a Munich surgeon who helped bring antiseptic surgery into Germany. Born in 1829, he studied at Munich. He traveled to study under leading surgeons in Paris, Berlin, and Wurzburg. In 1860 he became professor of surgery at Munich, a chair he kept for close to thirty years. His lectures were prized for their practical cast.

After studying under Spencer Wells in England he advanced pelvic surgery, and after learning antisepsis from Lister he spread it through German surgical clinics. His guide to antiseptic wound treatment ran through five editions and was translated into several languages. Among nearly a hundred publications, the best known dealt with ovariotomy, bone transplantation, hernia operations, and cancer treatment. He also served as consultant surgeon-general to Bavarian troops in the war of 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-of-ecl:
Julian of Eclanum was the most learned leader of the Pelagian movement. Born about 386, son of Memorius, a bishop in Apulia, he rose through lector and deacon to Bishop of Eclanum about 417. When Pope Zosimus condemned Pelagius in 418, Julian stood among eighteen Italian bishops who refused to sign, and Emperor Honorius exiled them.

Driven from Italy in 421, Julian systematized the teachings of Pelagius and Coelestius and became the party's intellectual chief. For years the struggle was largely a duel between Julian and Augustine, whose works quote Julian's lost books at length. Julian sought reopening of the case under each new pope and met fresh condemnations until his death in Sicily in 454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liber-diurnus: This 1913 reference piece on the Liber Diurnus — the papal formulary. Johann Peter Kirsch honors its famous formulas. Its pages framed the Roman chancery. The scholars prized the ancient book. The archives keep its name. Its 8th-century formulas are famed. Its 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-sc: This 1913 reference piece on the Scillitan Martyrs — the African twelve. Maurice Hassett unfolds their fateful tale. They sealed the faith with blood. The Church keeps the holy names. The second century knew their deaths. Their 180 deaths are famed. Their 180 martyrdoms are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menologium: This 1913 reference article on the Menologium — the Greek calendar. Herbert Thurston unfolds its liturgical lore. It lists the saints' feast-days. The East prizes the seemly book. The choirs keep its form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its saintly lists are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milevum: A 1913 entry on Milevum — a vanished Numidian see. Siméon Vailhé traces its fragmentary past. Prelates once shepherded the African faithful. Scant records preserve its story. Rome now lists it among titular sees. Its forgotten prelates are famed. Its titular status is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myriophytum: Myriophytum was an ancient city important enough to host a Christian bishop in the early centuries, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its church history. A quiet name from the ancient map, its bishops recorded in the old lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nahum: Nahum prophesied the fall of Nineveh, the bloody city, with poetry of terrifying power. This entry examines his short book, its historical setting, and its message. The prophet of the city's doom: his oracle against Nineveh is poetry of judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neum: The neum is the medieval note of Gregorian chant, the little sign that taught singers the melody before the staff existed. This entry explains its forms, its history, and its decipherment. The DNA of Western music: their shapes evolved into the notes we read today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitia-digni: The Notitia Dignitatum is the Roman Empire's great staff list, naming every office from Britain to Egypt around 400. This entry explains its contents, its date, and its value to historians. The empire's organization chart: its lists reveal Rome's late administration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitiae-epis: The Notitiae Episcopatuum were the Byzantine lists ranking every bishopric of the Eastern Empire. This entry explains their compilation, their order, and their value to historians. The empire's ecclesiastical directory: their rankings settled questions of precedence for centuries in the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-octavarium-ro: The Octavarium Romanum was the book of offices for the octaves of the great feasts. This entry explains its contents, its history, and its place in the liturgical books. Eight days of prayer, in print: its offices adorned the Church's greatest feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostensorium: The ostensorium is the monstrance that displays the Blessed Sacrament for adoration. This entry explains its forms, its history, and its use. The vessel of the visible Host: its sunburst of pure gold frames the Eucharistic Lord for the adoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pallium: The pallium is the woolen band the pope gives to archbishops, the symbol of their communion with Rome. This entry explains its form, its history, and its meaning. The yoke of the shepherd: its lamb's wool symbolizes the Good Shepherd.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraetonium: Paraetonium was a city of ancient Egypt important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the North African coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parium: Parium was a city of ancient Mysia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelusium: Pelusium was the great frontier city of the Nile delta, and its bishopric survives as a titular see. This entry covers its history, its bishops, and its ruins. The key of Egypt: its mighty fortress guarded the delta's eastern gate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philomelium: Philomelium was a city of ancient Phrygia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian plateau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenarium: This article treats its liturgical subject with the 1913 editors' characteristic thoroughness, tracing its history, its forms, and its significance in the Church's worship. A specialized entry from the encyclopedia's reference volumes, treated here with the encyclopedia's own scholarly care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polemonium: Polemonium was a city of the ancient Black Sea coast important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Pontic shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polystylum: Polystylum was a city of the ancient world important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the ancient map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pretorium: The Pretorium was Pilate's palace where Christ was judged. This entry discusses its site, its history, and the traditions. The hall of the Ecce Homo: its ancient stones heard the unjust sentence of Pilate himself in old Jerusalem's crowded court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proprium: The Proprium is the proper of the Mass and Office for the day. This entry explains its parts, its books, and its use. The day's own liturgy: its changing texts change with each feast of the turning year in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prum: Prüm was the great Benedictine abbey of the Eifel. This entry traces its foundation, its abbots, and its fortunes. The monastery of the Holy Saviour: its princely abbots ruled the Eifel hills for centuries in peace and prayer and song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prusias-ad-hy: Prusias ad Hypium, the Bithynian city on the Hypius river, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its ruins and its early church history. A quiet name from Asia Minor: its forgotten bishops signed the ancient councils of the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalterium: The Psalterium is the book of the 150 psalms for the Office. This entry explains its divisions, its history, and its use. The monks' breviary: its ordered weeks cycle the 150 psalms in turn unceasing forevermore in monastic choir and cell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratio-studior: The Ratio Studiorum is the Jesuits' plan of studies. This entry explains its method, its classes, and its influence. The curriculum of the Society: its ordered classes trained the Jesuit scholars of Europe's great colleges in Latin and Greek and rhetoric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regino-of-pru: Regino of Prüm was the chronicler-abbot of the tenth century. This entry notes his chronicle, his canon law, and his influence. The annalist of the Carolingians: his great chronicle spans the Frankish empire's fall in the 900s' wars and woes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-novarum: Rerum Novarum was Leo XIII's charter of labor. This entry examines its teachings, its impact, and its legacy. The magna carta of the workingman: its brave words freed the laborer in 1891's May of hope and justice and right and truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-responsorium: The responsorium is the sung answer of the Office. This entry explains its form, its history, and its music. The chant of response: its musical answer follows the lesson in choir and stall and nave in turn and time and tune.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-gloriose-: Rex gloriose martyrum is the hymn of the martyrs' King. This entry explains its text, its use, and its music. The hymn of the crowned witnesses: its solemn notes honor the slain for Christ in song and praise and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-sempitern: Rex sempiterne caelitum is the Easter hymn of the eternal King. This entry explains its text, its theme, and its music. The hymn of the risen Lord: its bright alleluias greet the Easter dawn in choir and chapel and home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robber-counci: The Robber Council of Ephesus was the violent synod of 449. This entry traces its doings, its condemnation, and its infamy. The council of the cudgels: its hired monks beat the bishops in 449's August heat in Ephesus's church of Mary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schola-cantor: The Schola Cantorum was the papal choir. This entry explains its origin, its singers, and its history. The singers of the Roman liturgy: their sweet chant fills the basilicas in Rome's churches in the 600s' decades of the popes in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptorium: The scriptorium was the writing room of the monastery. This entry explains its work, its scribes, and its history. The workshop of the medieval book: its long desks filled the cloister in the 1100s' abbeys of the monks in the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sirmium: Sirmium, the Pannonian city of the Sava, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Danube: its ancient ruins crown the Sava in Pannonia's plain in the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isidore-of: St. Isidore of Pelusium was the abbot of the Egyptian desert. This entry traces his letters, his Cyril, and his fame. The theologian of the Nile monks: his two thousand letters filled Pelusium in the 400s of the desert in the cells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-maris-mar: Maris, Martha, Audifax and Abachum were the Persian martyrs. This entry traces their Rome, their Aurelian, and their crowns. The family of the eastern faith: their martyr's blood sealed Rome in the 270 of the Aurelian in the city of the Caesars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syntagma-cano: The Syntagma Canonum is the collection of canons. This entry traces its Blastares and its Byzantine law. The code of the Eastern church: its many canons crowned Byzantium in the 1300s' empire in the east of the very old world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-targum: The Targum is the Aramaic paraphrase. This long entry examines its Onkelos, its synagogues, and its history. The translation of the Hebrew Bible: its old Aramaic crowned the synagogues in the 100s' Babylon in the exile of the old Jews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tavium: Tavium was the titular see of Galatia. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Asia Minor: its ancient ruins crowned Galatia in the books of the geographers in the library of the old scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-deum: The Te Deum is the hymn of thanksgiving. This long entry examines its Ambrose, its liturgy, and its music. The song of the Christian triumph: its great verses crowned the liturgy in the 400s' Milan in the basilica of the Ambrosians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-lucis-ante: Te Lucis Ante Terminum is the Compline hymn. This entry traces its words, its night, and its music. The prayer before the light fails: its quiet verses crowned Compline in the 500s' night in the choir of the old monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-coliseum: The Coliseum was the arena of Rome. This long entry examines its Vespasian, its martyrs, and its history. The amphitheatre of the Flavians: its vast arches crowned Rome in the 70s of the Flavians in the truly very old valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-martyrs-o: The martyrs of Gorkum were the nineteen of 1572. This entry traces their Brielle, their Eucharist, and their fame. The confessors of the Dutch revolt: their dark prison crowned Brielle in the 1572 of the Sea Beggars in the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-themisonium: Themisonium was the titular see of Pisidia. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Asia Minor: its ancient ruins crowned Pisidia in the books of the Strabo in the truly very old high hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-of-s: Theodore the Studite was the monk of the icons. This very long entry examines his 700s, his Studion, and his exile. The champion of the holy images: his great Studion crowned Constantinople in the 700s of the Irene in the monastery.
doe-osti-3001271-ab-initio-equation-of-s: Vanadium got its ab initio equation, and this DOE report computes the state from theory. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their numbers. The element was vanadium. The numbers were physicist. The theory was ab initio. The numbers were theory.
doe-osti-3014292-baseline-cost-model-for: Hydropower costs got baseline-modeled, and this DOE 2025 documentation covers the model. The pages detail the findings. The hydro folks get their data. The year was 2025. The data were hydro. The documentation was model. The model was baseline. The year was DOE's.
doe-osti-3020149-expanding-the-boundarie: Transuranium got boundary-expanded, and this DOE text pushes the chemistry frontier. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their data. The chemistry was transuranium. The data were chemist. The frontier was chemistry. The DOE was text. The chemistry was DOE.
doe-osti-3021386-lithium-divertor-intera: Lithium divertors got helium-trapped, and this DOE final studies lithiated metals. The pages detail the technical findings. The fusion folks get their closeout. The trapping was hydrogen. The closeout was fusion. The metals were lithiated. The report was technical.
doe-osti-3395071-steady-state-radiolysis: Polyhalides got radiolysis-accumulated, and this DOE poster covers steady state products. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their deck. The format was poster. The deck was chemist. The accumulation were products. The steady were state. The poster were format.
govdocs-archive_org-the-complete-books-o:
Charles Fort collected facts that science would not touch: rains of frogs, objects falling from clear skies, people vanishing and reappearing. The Complete Books of Charles Fort joins his four works in one volume: The Book of the Damned, New Lands, Lo!, and Wild Talents.

Fort called his outcast facts damned data, and he presented them with wit and open contempt for smug experts. He did not prove a theory; he proved a habit of ignoring. That stance made him the father of fortean inquiry, and his books still supply the field's founding cases and its fighting tone.
history-of-the-britons-historia-brittonu:
Nennius, who calls himself a lowly minister and disciple of Saint Elbotus, compiled the History of the Britons in Latin, here translated by J A Giles. His prologue confesses dull intellect and rude speech, and says he gathered the work from ancestors' traditions, writings, and monuments. It is less a history than a heap of British antiquities.

The text gives the Romans, the Saxon advent under Hengist, who demands Kent as his daughter's price through an interpreter, Saint Patrick, and Vortigern. Arthur appears as a war leader winning twelve battles, the earliest Arthur in any history. Brief and credulous as it is, the Historia Brittonum shaped Geoffrey of Monmouth and every later British chronicle.
nasa-tm-19650010883-analysis-of-oxygen-i:
Glenn R Zellars compiled the minutes of a NASA round-robin meeting held at Lewis Research Center on June 4, 1964. The subject was measuring oxygen inside potassium metal. Several labs had each analyzed the same potassium samples, then compared results. Groups taking part included Dow Chemical, General Electric, Oak Ridge, and Pratt and Whitney.

Two methods were in use, mercury amalgamation and vacuum distillation. A round-robin test shows whether different labs get the same answer. If they do not, the method needs work. Minutes like these preserve that check in detail, including who took part and what was discussed at the meeting.
nasa-tm-19680001040-thermal-contact-cond:
Harry L. Atkins, of the Space Thermodynamics Branch at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports contract results on how heat crosses a touching joint in vacuum. Two surfaces bolted together pass heat only at scattered contact points. In space, no air helps, so the joint's conductance must be known.

The work plots conductance against applied pressure for four metals. Stainless steel, magnesium, aluminum, and copper samples all appear. Atkins also studies a kink in the aluminum curves when plotted on log-log paper. Squashed cones, hemispheres, and ellipses reproduce the same kink, suggesting scaled-up models of real contact points.
nasa-tm-19680020447-back-flow-from-jet-p:
Norman T. Grier of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52468, for a July 1968 symposium on rarefied gas dynamics in Cambridge, Massachusetts. His concern is back flow: exhaust gas from a rocket jet that spreads backward in vacuum. Such gas can coat or disturb the very spacecraft that fired the jet.

Grier estimates the back flow density at points level with the nozzle exit plane. His model treats the young plume as a smooth gas flow, then as free flying particles once the gas grows too thin for collisions. He runs the approximate calculation for helium, nitrogen, and argon jets. The result is a practical way to judge a plume's backward reach.
nasa-tm-19690028938-tensile-properties-o:
Adolph C. Spagnuolo and Phillip L. Stone of Lewis Research Center measured the pull strength of pure tantalum in this September 1969 memo. Samples of varied shapes and from varied heats were pulled at high heat. Tests ran in hard vacuum to shield the metal from air.

Peak stress values spread widely among sample shapes at the top test heat. Samples cut from the same heat, by contrast, matched each other well. Tube samples from one heat sat in a narrow strength band. The spread warns engineers to rate tantalum by heat and form, not by book values alone. Tantalum serves in hot aerospace and nuclear gear.
nasa-tm-19700017669-effect-of-adding-lit:
John L. Anderson and Wendell Mayo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in May 1970. It studies a fast-spectrum nuclear critical assembly ringed by molybdenum. The team added four materials, one at a time, and watched the effects.

The added materials were lithium nitride, hafnium, tantalum, and tungsten. For each case the report tracks the fuel loading the assembly needed. It also tracks the resulting neutron energy spectrum, the spread of neutron speeds inside. Such tests guide the design of compact reactors, where each added material changes how the core behaves.
nasa-tm-19710019446-quenching-of-vacanci:
H H Grimes and E R Gotsky of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a September 1971 meeting in Mol, Belgium, on defects in refractory metals. It concerns vacancies, the empty spots left when atoms are missing from a crystal. The team quenched molybdenum, freezing vacancies in place for study. Such defects shape radiation damage, diffusion, and strength in hot metals.

Fast quenching into ultrapure liquid helium had worked well for tungsten. That cold bath keeps the metal clean during the plunge. Earlier teams used the method to measure the energy needed to form a vacancy. Grimes and Gotsky applied the approach to molybdenum, a body centered cubic metal. Their work extended a proven technique to a new material.
pax-vobiscum:
Henry Drummond published Pax Vobiscum in 1890, the second of a series that began with "The Greatest Thing in the World." The title takes Christ's words, "Peace be with you." The book opens on his promise of rest to all who labour and are heavy laden.

Drummond complains that popular religion uses great words like rest, joy, and peace without saying how to get them. His chapters, with titles like "Effects Require Causes" and "How Fruits Grow," try to give working answers. He writes as a scientist and a preacher at once, in short, plain chapters.
peeps-at-many-lands-belgium: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Peeps at Many Lands: Belgium, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names George W. T. Omond as author and Amédée Forestier as illustrator, published in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1909. The contents cover the Flemish plain, Belgian towns and the Ardennes, children and their festivals, Christmas and carnival, the languages spoken, a short history, and the Belgian army and the Congo.
podcast-dannyjones-7RD8FxI0yuM:
Greg Carlwood hosts a long-running conspiracy podcast of his own. On Danny Jones's show the two hosts trade territory. Their subject is the darkest conspiracies in the world, as Carlwood's years of interviews have mapped them. The episode is a tour led by a man who has heard nearly every theory in circulation.

Carlwood ranks and connects the claims, from secret societies to hidden history, with the ease of a guide who knows which doors open and which are painted on. Jones, playing guest in spirit, asks the questions his own listeners would ask. Nothing here is verified, and both men treat the material as a landscape of belief rather than a court record. That is the point of the archive copy: a map of modern conspiracy culture drawn by one of its native guides.
podcast-tuckercarlson-r_eFGCBPuuM:
Saudi investor Prince Alwaleed bin Talal talks with Tucker Carlson about markets, media, and change. Alwaleed built wealth over four decades and once held a large stake in Fox News. He later backed the platform X.

He says he feels hopeful as a new Trump term begins. The pair discuss tariffs, debt, and border policy in broad terms. They also touch on DeepSeek and the race in smart software. The episode offers a rare long interview with a royal investor who has bet on media and tech for years. Few guests bring his mix of royal rank and market skill.
rejected-addresses-or-the-new-theatrum-p:
James Smith and Horace Smith wrote the mock addresses in this book, here in a new edition from John Murray of London in 1879. Lord Byron's letters to Murray from October 1812 are printed at the front in praise. Byron forgave the brothers for their satire and thought their imitations first-rate.

He called the book the best thing of its kind since The Rolliad, and the best imitations ever made of hard originals. The pieces were addresses meant for a theatre opening, cast in the styles of famed poets of the day. Their wit made the brothers' name, and Murray's edition keeps Byron's verdict as its warrant.
specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-known: Rev. George Gilfillan edits Volume II of Specimens with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets, in a set of three volumes, with a first essay of his own. The contents place this book in the second period, from Spenser to Dryden, continued. William Habington comes first, with a letter to the Honorable W. E. and A Description of Castara. Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich, gives two satires, and Richard Lovelace gives songs that name To Althea, from Prison, and A Loose Saraband.
symposium:
Plato's Symposium appears here in Benjamin Jowett's English translation, with Jowett's long introduction at its head. Jowett calls the dialogue the most perfect in form of all Plato's works, a work holding more than any commentator has dreamed of and more, perhaps, than the author himself knew.

He insists that Plato was no mystic. He was no sentimentalist either. Eastern influences never touched him, though they later spread over the Alexandrian world. The Symposium is Greek in style and subject. It has a beauty as of a statue. The dialogue itself reports a drinking party. Socrates and his friends make speeches in praise of love. The playwright Aristophanes is among them. The young Alcibiades comes late. Each speaker tops the last. At the end Socrates reports the teaching of Diotima.
tanakh-jps-1917-nahum:
Nahum is a brief prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English rendering. It is called the burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.

God is shown as slow to anger yet great in power, who will not clear the guilty. His path lies in whirlwind and storm, with clouds as the dust of his feet, and seas dry up at his rebuke. The verse then turns its force on Nineveh, the vast Assyrian capital, and foretells her fall. Readers get fierce, compact poetry of doom for a cruel empire, paired with relief for Judah, long crushed under its yoke.
the-adventures-of-unc-billy-possum: With art by Harrison Cady, The Adventures of Unc' Billy Possum joins Thornton W. Burgess's Bedtime Story-Books. Little, Brown, and Company printed it at Boston in 1920. Chapters listed open with Unc' Billy caught. Reddy Fox then thinks he sees a ghost. Unc' Billy sends for his family next. Bobby Coon enters the wrong house after that. A runaway cabbage stands near the end.
the-camp-fire-girls-on-the-farm-or-bessi:
Jane L. Stewart wrote The Camp Fire Girls on the Farm, or Bessie King's New Chum, volume two of the Camp Fire Girls Series. The Saalfield Publishing Company put it out, with rights dated 1914. A plate shows a girl turning to look up into the evil eyes of Farmer Weeks. Chapter I is called In the City.

Bessie King speaks first, eyes open with admiration and wonder. She asks her chum Zara if she ever dreamed of such a lovely room. The room is in the home of Eleanor Mercer, Guardian of the Manasquan Camp Fire. Both girls are new members of the organization. Bessie has lived all her life in the country, and has known nothing of the luxuries city girls take as a matter of course. In Mercer's house she has found something new to astonish her in almost every room.
the-courage-of-captain-plum:
James Oliver Curwood's The Courage of Captain Plum, dated 1912 with pictures by Frank E. Schoonover, opens in the early summer of 1856. Captain Nathaniel Plum, master and owner of the sloop Typhoon, sits hidden on Beaver Island, smoking an enormous pipe and watching Lake Michigan at sunset.

Plum is eight or nine and twenty, lean and tanned, full of good humor, though his thoughts run on an unpleasant subject. Three miles off, his sloop rides between two islands, and no other sail is in sight. Trees and vines screen his back, so only a boat edging close around the island's end could find him. He knocks out his pipe on his boot-heel and checks a long-barreled revolver, powder and ball, with care.
the-dash-for-khartoum:
G. A. Henty's The Dash for Khartoum, a tale of the Nile Expedition dated 1892, was published in London by Blackie and Son with ten page illustrations by Joseph Nash and John Schonberg. A publisher's list at the front prices his other historical tales, from The Cat of Bubastes to With Clive in India, at five or six shillings each.

In a preface addressed My Dear Lads, Henty says the Nile Expedition is too recent to need historical introduction. His moral concerns two lads brought up as brothers: never act in haste, for repentance follows. A generous impulse can mislead as surely as an evil one, he warns, and hiding trouble from a father or best friend springs from cowardice. Lay the case frankly before your natural advisers, he urges, and bear their displeasure rather than risk lasting injury.
the-love-sonnets-of-a-hoodlum:
Wallace Irwin's The Love Sonnets of a Hoodlum opens with an introduction by Gelett Burgess on the sonnet itself. Burgess calls the sonnet cycle the highest form lyric passion has reached, likening a sonnet to a crystal goblet holding one inspired thought so perfectly that another drop would overflow. He traces the form from Dante, Petrarch, and Camoens through Shakespeare, then to Rossetti, Browning, and Meredith in the Victorian era.

Into that polished line steps slang. Burgess argues that the twentieth century's new influence is the enthusiasm of slang, which has slowly won verbs, nouns, idiom, and diction. His subtitle promises to show how vanity is still on deck and humble virtue gets it in the neck. The introduction presents street language as fresh blood for a conventional, thinning literary style.
the-works-of-francis-beaumont-and-john-f: Volume one of The Works of Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher gives their birth and death dates on its title pages. Beaumont lived from 1584 to 1616, Fletcher from 1579 to 1625. Five plays are named, including The Maid's Tragedy and Philaster. Arnold Glover edited the text. A note begins by describing the first collected edition of 1647. That folio's size and title page are recorded for collation. The plays themselves start beyond the pages shown here.
vera-the-medium:
Richard Harding Davis opens Vera, the Medium with a newspaper making the most of a scoop. The Despatch has spread the name of Stephen Hallowell, his portrait, and a picture of his house across three columns, under the words At Point of Death. Yet the news lands flat in New York. Only city editors, vexed at missing it, and railroad presidents, figuring fast on slips of paper, take much notice.

Davis explains the coolness. In the early eighties Hallowell had been a national figure, a power in western railroads and eastern markets, when a few millions still counted as colossal wealth. His start came from a patent coupling pin devised by his brother-in-law, which he pushed on the new western roads. Twenty years on, greater giants have dwarfed him. The tale turns to the medium Vera, and to what a dying man's fortune draws out of people.
